youtube.baslik: The Middle Ear Cavity: Walls and Neighbors | Lesson 19 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
The air-filled space behind the tympanic membrane, the tympanic cavity, is small but very important. In this lesson we cover the epitympanum, mesotympanum and hypotympanum, the six walls and their neighboring structures, and the link to the mastoid antrum. We also see how these relate to tympanometry and clinical practice.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Gray's Anatomy; Zemlin, Speech and Hearing Science: Anatomy and Physiology; Seikel, King and Drumright, Anatomy and Physiology for Speech, Language, and Hearing; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Its levels, six walls and neighbors
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will examine the air-filled space behind the tympanic membrane: the middle ear cavity.
We will learn the levels of the cavity, its six walls and the important structures those walls border.

cumleler.yazi: Behind the tympanic membrane, inside the temporal bone, lies the tympanic cavity, the cavum tympani.

cumleler: The tympanic membrane lies on the outer side of the cavity, and the inner ear lies on its inner side.
The cavity is filled with air and lined by a thin mucosa.
In front it opens to the nasopharynx through the Eustachian tube, and behind it opens to the mastoid air cells.
Through these connections, the middle ear becomes part of an air system whose air is renewed.

maddeler.metin: Width at the center: only _2 mm_

cumleler: Seen from the side, the middle ear cavity looks like a tall box; seen from the front, it is very narrow.
Its height and its front-to-back depth are about fifteen millimeters.
Its width, however, is very small: at the center, between the umbo and the medial wall, only about two millimeters.
The width increases to about six millimeters at the top and about four millimeters at the bottom.
This narrow space holds the ossicles, two small muscles, nerves and blood vessels.
Because the space is narrow, the structures on the medial wall lie just behind the eardrum; this matters in the clinic.

notlar.metin: Attic: the level _opening to the mastoid_

cumleler: The middle ear cavity is divided into three levels relative to the tympanic membrane.

cumleler.yazi: The part above the upper edge of the eardrum is the epitympanum, or attic; the malleus head and the incus body lie here.
The main part at the level of the eardrum is the mesotympanum; the stapes, the windows and the muscle tendons are at this level.
The shallow part below the lower edge of the eardrum is the hypotympanum.
Some sources also define the area around the tube opening as the protympanum, and the posterior part as the retrotympanum.
The epitympanum holds the passage to the mastoid, so it plays a special role in the spread of disease.

cumleler: We can think of the middle ear cavity as a box with six walls.
Its roof is a thin plate of bone called the tegmen tympani, which separates the cavity from the middle cranial fossa.
Its floor is separated by thin bone from the widened part of the internal jugular vein, the jugular bulb.
The lower part of the anterior wall borders the internal carotid artery; the Eustachian tube and the tensor tympani canal open above.
The posterior wall has a passage that opens to the mastoid antrum.
The lateral wall is formed mostly by the tympanic membrane, while the medial wall faces the inner ear.
The medial wall is the richest wall of the middle ear, because it borders the inner ear directly.
The rounded bulge in the middle is the promontory; it is formed by the basal turn of the cochlea bulging into the middle ear.
Behind and above the promontory is the fenestra vestibuli, the oval window, where the stapes footplate sits.

cumleler.yazi: Behind and below it is the fenestra cochleae, the round window, which is closed by a thin membrane.

cumleler: The bony canal of the facial nerve runs just above the oval window.
Above that, we see the bulge formed by the lateral semicircular canal.
In front of the oval window is a small bony projection around which the tensor tympani tendon turns.
The tegmen tympani that forms the roof is very thin; in some people there may even be small gaps in the bone.
So neglected middle ear infections can, though rarely, spread to the meninges and the temporal lobe.
The floor is also separated from the jugular bulb by thin bone.
In some people the bulb sits high and may be seen as a bluish shadow behind the eardrum.
The internal carotid artery rises in a bony canal in the lower part of the anterior wall; the Eustachian tube opens in the upper part.
These neighbors explain why great care is needed in middle ear surgery.
Most of the lateral wall is formed by the tympanic membrane.

cumleler.yazi: Above the upper edge of the eardrum is a thin bony rim that forms the lateral wall of the epitympanum; this is called the scutum.
Between the pars flaccida and the neck of the malleus lies a small area called Prussak's space.
Cholesteatoma arising from the pars flaccida usually starts in this area and can erode the scutum.

cumleler: This erosion is an important finding that can be seen on computed tomography.

sahneler.baslik: Posterior wall: the passage to the *mastoid*

cumleler.yazi: In the upper part of the posterior wall, a passage runs back from the epitympanum; it is called the aditus ad antrum.

cumleler: This passage opens into the largest air space in the mastoid, the antrum mastoideum, or mastoid antrum.
The mastoid antrum is already present at birth.
The small air cells that spread out from the antrum develop after birth; this is called pneumatization.
The development of these cells continues through childhood and varies greatly from person to person.
The middle ear, antrum and mastoid cells share the same mucosal lining, so a middle ear infection can spread to the mastoid.
The mastoid cells act like an air reservoir for the middle ear and help buffer pressure changes.
On the posterior wall is a small bony projection called the pyramidal eminence.
The stapedius muscle lies inside this eminence, and its tendon runs from the tip to the stapes.
The facial nerve descends deep in the posterior wall and leaves the temporal bone through a foramen in the skull base.

cumleler.yazi: Its branch, the chorda tympani, crosses the middle ear near the eardrum and carries taste from the front of the tongue.

cumleler: The change in taste sometimes seen after middle ear surgery is related to this thin nerve.
The mucosa lining the middle ear cavity has the same origin as the mucosa of the nose and pharynx.
Ciliated cells are found especially near the Eustachian tube, and they carry secretions toward the tube.
The rich network of blood vessels in the mucosa constantly absorbs some of the gas in the cavity into the blood.
Because of this absorption, pressure in a closed middle ear gradually becomes negative.
Regular opening of the Eustachian tube replaces this loss; we will look at how this works in a later lesson.
These features of the mucosa also explain why the middle ear can collect fluid so easily.
An air-filled middle ear cavity is needed for the eardrum to vibrate freely.
Tympanometry shows this indirectly: when the cavity is filled with air, a normal, peaked curve is obtained.
When the cavity fills with fluid, eardrum movement decreases and the curve flattens.
Because the cavity is so narrow, even a small amount of fluid can clearly affect eardrum movement.
If the eardrum is perforated, the device also measures the middle ear cavity and mastoid cells, so the measured volume is large.

sahneler.metin: If you see a reddish mass or a bluish shadow behind the eardrum, record it. Pulse-synchronous ripples on the tympanogram are also an important clue.
cumleler: A tip from practice: because the eardrum is thin and translucent, the space behind it can sometimes be seen during otoscopy.
If you see a reddish mass or a bluish shadow behind the eardrum, be sure to record it.
Small ripples on the curve that are synchronous with the pulse during tympanometry are also a finding worth noting.
These findings may be related to vascular structures; the person is referred to a physician for evaluation.

cumleler.yazi: Relative to the eardrum, the middle ear cavity is divided into three levels: epitympanum, mesotympanum and hypotympanum.

cumleler: Thin bone separates its roof, the tegmen tympani, from the middle cranial fossa, and its floor from the jugular bulb.
The medial wall holds the promontory, the oval window, the round window and the canal of the facial nerve.
The aditus ad antrum in the posterior wall connects the cavity with the mastoid antrum and air cells.

sahneler.soru: What separates the middle ear from the middle cranial fossa?
sahneler.aciklama: The _tegmen tympani_ that forms the roof is a thin bony plate; the middle cranial fossa lies beyond it.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: Which thin bony plate separates the middle ear cavity from the middle cranial fossa?
The correct answer is B: the tegmen tympani.

cumleler: The tegmen tympani is the roof of the cavity; because it is so thin, it is clinically important.
